title: 22. Interview: Logging
summary: Interview Q&A for Logging — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Logging interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between structured and unstructured logging, and why does it matter at scale?
**Answer:** Unstructured logs are free-form text strings written for human readability, like `"User 42 logged in"`. Structured logs are JSON objects with explicit fields, like `{"event":"login","user_id":42,"ip":"1.2.3.4"}`. The difference matters because aggregators can index structured fields into B-trees and answer boolean queries in milliseconds, whereas unstructured logs require full-text substring scans across billions of lines, which is orders of magnitude slower and more error-prone. At Netflix scale — trillions of events per day — the difference between a 200ms structured query and a 30-second grep is the difference between an engineer fixing the bug tonight or going home frustrated. Structured logs also compress better and propagate types (numbers stay numbers), enabling downstream alerting on numeric fields. The trade-off is developer friction: every new field must be declared and propagated, and sloppy field naming causes query inconsistency across teams.

**Visual:**
```
Unstructured: "User 42 logged in from 1.2.3.4 at 03:14"
Structured:   {"user_id":42,"ip":"1.2.3.4","event":"login","ts":"03:14"}

Query "all logins from 1.2.3.4":
  Unstructured: grep "1.2.3.4" *.log        (slow, false positives)
  Structured:   WHERE ip = "1.2.3.4"         (indexed, fast)
```

### Q2. Explain the standard log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL) and a policy for using each.
**Answer:** DEBUG captures internal state useful only during development or deep diagnosis — cache hits/misses, internal branch decisions. INFO records normal lifecycle events that an operator expects to see in steady state — server start, request received, order completed. WARN flags abnormal but recoverable behavior — retries, degraded fallback, rate-limited calls. ERROR marks a failed operation that needs human attention but did not crash the process — a 502 from a dependency, a failed DB write that was retried. FATAL is reserved for unrecoverable failures that force process exit — cannot bind to required port, cannot load mandatory config. A sound policy is: ERROR must be pageable if it fires above a threshold rate, FATAL must page immediately, WARN must be reviewable weekly, and DEBUG must be off by default in production. The common anti-pattern is logging every caught exception as ERROR, which trains on-call engineers to ignore the channel.

**Visual:**
```
FATAL  --> process exits, page immediately
ERROR  --> pageable, runbook link required
WARN   --> reviewable, weekly digest
INFO   --> normal events, always on
DEBUG  --> off in prod, on during diagnosis
```

### Q3. What is log cardinality, and why is it dangerous?
**Answer:** Cardinality is the number of distinct values a field can take. A field like `http_status` has cardinality ~60, which is cheap to index. A field like `user_id` at Netflix has cardinality 260 million, which is expensive in any system that aggregates by that field. In logs, high cardinality is acceptable because log stores are designed for full-text retrieval, not for computing time series per distinct value. The danger appears when teams try to derive metrics from high-cardinality log fields — for example, counting requests per `session_id` per minute creates an unbounded time series that explodes memory in Prometheus, Datadog, or M3. A real case in 2020 saw an e-commerce team's Datadog bill jump from $40K to $1.2M in one month because a debug log line containing a per-session UUID was accidentally parsed as a metric label. The rule: logs are for high-cardinality events you retrieve individually; metrics are for low-cardinality aggregates you sum or histogram across.

**Visual:**
```
Field          Cardinality     Safe in metrics?
http_status    ~60             yes
route          ~500            yes
user_id        260,000,000     NO  (use in logs only)
session_id     unbounded       NO  (use in logs only)
```

### Q4. Compare head-based and tail-based log sampling. When would you use each?
**Answer:** Head-based sampling decides at log emission time whether to keep a record, typically by hashing a trace ID deterministically so the same request is fully logged or fully dropped across all services. It is simple, stateless, and cheap, but it samples blindly — it discards 99% of errors just as readily as 99% of healthy requests. Tail-based sampling waits until the request completes, then makes a retention decision based on the outcome: keep 100% of errors and slow outliers, drop 90% of fast successes. This preserves all interesting events while reducing volume dramatically, at the cost of buffering the entire request's logs in memory until completion and adding a decision stage to the pipeline. Netflix's pipeline uses tail-based sampling at the edge, achieving 90%+ volume reduction without losing incident visibility. Use head-based sampling when volume is moderate and you trust random sampling to capture rare events; use tail-based when volume is extreme and you cannot afford to drop errors.

**Visual:**
```
Head-based (decide at start):
  req arrives --> hash(trace_id)%100 < 1? --> keep all logs of req
  Pros: stateless  Cons: drops errors too

Tail-based (decide at end):
  req completes --> err? latency>p99? --> keep  else drop 90%
  Pros: keeps all interesting  Cons: needs buffering
```

### Q5. How do correlation IDs (trace IDs) propagate across microservices, and why are they essential for logging?
**Answer:** A correlation ID is a unique identifier generated at the edge of the system (typically by the API gateway or first service) and propagated to every downstream service via a request header like `X-Request-ID` or `traceparent` (per W3C Trace Context). Each service reads the header on entry, attaches it to every log line as a structured field, and forwards it unchanged on outbound calls. This lets an engineer query the central log aggregator for a single ID and reconstruct the entire path the request took — service A called B which called C which timed out — in seconds. Without correlation IDs, reconstructing a multi-hop failure requires time-window heuristics that miss concurrent requests and produce false matches. Uber's migration to TChannel in 2016 and the industry-wide adoption of OpenTelemetry trace propagation in 2020 were both driven largely by the operational impossibility of debugging microservices without a propagated ID.

**Visual:**
```
Gateway: X-Request-ID: abc-123
  --> SvcA (log: req_id=abc-123)
        --> SvcB (log: req_id=abc-123)
              --> SvcC (log: req_id=abc-123, ERROR timeout)

Query:  WHERE req_id = "abc-123"  --> all three logs in one panel
```

### Q6. Compare the ELK stack, Grafana Loki, and Splunk as centralized log aggregation systems.
**Answer:** ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) builds an inverted index over every token of every log line, enabling fast full-text and structured queries, but at high storage and memory cost — typically 3–5x the raw log volume after indexing. Splunk is a proprietary system with the same inverted-index philosophy but with much stronger analytics (SPL pipeline language) and enterprise features like role-based access and audit; its licensing is expensive and typically priced per GB ingested. Grafana Loki takes a deliberately different approach: it indexes only a small set of labels (app, env, instance) and stores the raw log lines as compressed chunks in object storage, relying on brute-force grep for full-text search. This makes Loki 10–100x cheaper than ELK for the same volume, at the cost of slower substring queries. The choice is a trade-off: ELK/Splunk for ad-hoc forensic search across unknown fields, Loki when you already know which service and time window to investigate — which is the common case in incident response.

**Visual:**
```
ELK:        index every token, fast search, 3-5x storage cost
Splunk:     same + SPL analytics, $ per GB ingested, expensive
Loki:       index labels only, grep the rest, 10-100x cheaper
            (slower for ad-hoc substring across all fields)
```

### Q7. What is the difference between logs, metrics, and traces, and why are they called the three pillars of observability?
**Answer:** Logs are discrete, time-stamped records of individual events — they answer "what happened, in detail." Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time — they answer "how much, how fast, how often" without preserving individual events. Traces record the causal path of a single request across service boundaries — they answer "which service called which, and where did time go." They are called the three pillars because each captures a dimension the others lose: metrics are cheap to store and fast to alert on but discard individual events; logs preserve individual events but are too expensive to alert on at line volume; traces show causality and latency breakdown but only for sampled requests. A mature observability stack uses all three: metrics trigger the alert, traces show which service was slow, logs show why the service was slow. Grafana, Datadog, and Honeycomb all converged on this triad by 2022 because no single pillar is sufficient.

**Visual:**
```
Metrics:   rate, error, latency        (cheap, alertable, lossy)
Logs:      event detail                (expensive, searchable, lossless)
Traces:    causal path per request     (sampled, shows latency breakdown)

Alert fires on metric --> trace shows the slow span --> log shows why
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your team's Elasticsearch cluster keeps running out of disk. How do you reduce log volume without losing incident visibility?
**Answer:** First, audit log levels in production — many teams ship DEBUG logs to the central aggregator by default; flip those to INFO and require explicit opt-in for debug windows. Second, introduce tail-based sampling: keep 100% of ERROR and WARN logs, 100% of requests slower than p99 latency, and sample 1–10% of healthy INFO logs using a deterministic hash of the trace ID. Third, drop noisy low-value fields from the JSON payload (full request bodies, repetitive stack traces from known benign exceptions) and replace them with hashed references stored once. Fourth, enforce retention policies — 7 days hot, 30 days warm, 1 year cold in object storage — so the expensive Elasticsearch index holds only the hot tier. Fifth, identify the top volume sources with a quick aggregation; usually one or two chatty services dominate and can be throttled without affecting incident response. Netflix applied exactly this playbook in 2019 and cut log volume 70% while improving query latency because the smaller index fit in RAM.

**Visual:**
```
Before:  all logs -> ES index (10 TB/week, OOM)
After:   DEBUG off, INFO sampled 5%
         ERROR/WARN/slow=100%
         hot 7d / warm 30d / cold 1y
         Volume -70%, query latency -40%
```

### Q2. A new microservice your team launched is logging every caught exception as ERROR. The on-call team is threatening to mute the channel. What do you do?
**Answer:** This is a classic alert-fatigue scenario, and the fix is a log taxonomy, not a tooling change. First, sit with the team and classify each ERROR site: if the exception was caught and the operation was retried successfully, downgrade to WARN. If it was caught and a fallback path served the user correctly, downgrade to INFO with a `degraded=true` field. Reserve ERROR for cases where the operation failed and the user got an error response or the data was lost. Second, attach a `runbook_url` field to every ERROR so the on-call engineer can click straight to remediation steps. Third, set a rate-based alert on ERROR per service per minute — if it exceeds the steady-state baseline, page; otherwise, let it accumulate for the weekly review. Fourth, measure the change: after the reclassification, the page rate should drop 80%+ and the engineers should regain trust in the channel. The deeper lesson is that log levels are an SLA with the on-call team, and violating that SLA destroys the channel's value faster than any tooling limitation.

**Visual:**
```
Before:  every catch block -> ERROR -> 500 pages/day -> mutiny
After:   retried+ok     -> WARN
         fallback served -> INFO degraded=true
         user-visible failure -> ERROR + runbook_url
         page rate -80%, trust restored
```

### Q3. You join a startup where every microservice writes logs to its own local file and engineers SSH into boxes to grep them. How do you design a centralized logging pipeline?
**Answer:** The goal is to move logs off the boxes into a central, queryable store without rewriting applications. Step one: standardize on JSON output to stdout for every service, even if it means a small logging library refactor per language. Step two: deploy a lightweight node-level agent — Fluent Bit or Vector — as a DaemonSet on every Kubernetes node (or systemd unit on every VM) that tails stdout/container logs, attaches metadata (host, env, service name), and ships over TLS. Step three: choose a backend based on budget and query patterns — Grafana Loki for cost-efficient label-based queries, Elasticsearch for full-text forensic search, Splunk if enterprise procurement requires it. Step four: build a single Grafana or Kibana dashboard per service showing error rate, top error messages, and a log panel filtered by trace ID. Step five: enforce a correlation ID header (`X-Request-ID`) propagated from the gateway so cross-service queries work. Step six: set retention (7d hot, 30d warm, 1y cold) and alert on ingestion rate to catch runaway services early. This design is the de facto 2024 industry baseline.

**Visual:**
```
Service (stdout JSON)
   |
   v
Fluent Bit (DaemonSet) --tail--> Loki / ES
   |                              |
   v                              v
metadata: host, env, svc     Grafana dashboard
                                |
                                v
                          query by trace_id
```

### Q4. During a major outage, your log aggregator itself becomes unreachable. How do you design logging to survive this?
**Answer:** This is exactly the lesson of Facebook's October 2021 outage, where internal tooling died alongside the system it observed because everything shared the same DNS and network path. The fix is layered. First, the application must always write logs to a local file (or stdout) before any agent ships them, so logs survive even if the network is down — local disk is the durable buffer. Second, the shipping agent (Fluent Bit, Vector) must spool to disk when the central aggregator is unreachable, replaying when connectivity returns. Third, the aggregator itself must run in a separate failure domain — separate cluster, separate network, separate identity provider — so a BGP or DNS mistake in the production network does not take it down. Fourth, the most critical logs (audit, security, payment) should be shipped to two aggregators in different regions or even different providers. Fifth, the on-call runbook must include "logs aggregator down" as a top-level scenario with manual fallbacks: SSH to the box, read the local file directly. Logging infrastructure is itself a production system and needs the same resilience as the systems it observes.

**Visual:**
```
App --> local file (survives network outage)
         |
         v
       Fluent Bit --spool to disk if aggregator down--> retry
         |
         v
       Aggregator (separate failure domain, separate auth)
         |
         v
       Replica in region B (for audit/security logs)
```

### Q5. Your team wants to alert on log lines containing "payment failed" but the volume is too high to alert on every match. How do you design this?
**Answer:** Alerting on raw log substring matches is almost always wrong because it produces unactionable noise — every transient retry or expected decline fires a page. The correct design is to extract the signal from the log into a metric, then alert on the metric. Concretely: emit a structured log line `{"event":"payment_failed","reason":"insufficient_funds","amount":42}` and have the agent or a log-to-metric pipeline (Vector's `remap` + `metric`, or Prometheus' `loki.source.api`) increment a counter `payment_failed_total{reason="..."}`. Then alert on rate of change: `rate(payment_failed_total[5m]) > threshold` for a fixed threshold, or `increase(payment_failed_total[1h]) > 2 * historical_baseline` for an anomaly-style alert. Group by `reason` so the alert includes the breakdown. This combines logs' detail (the structured payload is still searchable) with metrics' aggregatability (the counter is cheap to alert on). The rule of thumb is: logs are for human forensics, metrics are for machine alerting — never alert directly on log substring matches.

**Visual:**
```
Wrong:  alert if log contains "payment failed"   (noisy)

Right:  log: {"event":"payment_failed","reason":"..."}
        -> extract to metric: payment_failed_total{reason}
        -> alert: rate()[5m] > threshold
        -> page includes reason breakdown
```

### Q6. You discover a service is logging full PII (emails, credit card numbers) to the central aggregator. What is your remediation plan?
**Answer:** This is a security and compliance incident, not just a logging issue. Step one: immediately identify the offending log lines and redact them at the source by patching the application's logger to scrub known PII fields (email, phone, SSN, card number) before emission — never rely on the central aggregator to redact, because logs already on disk or in agent buffers will leak. Step two: rotate the aggregator's storage for the affected time window — Elasticsearch indices can be deleted by date, Loki chunks by retention window — and verify with a full scan that no PII remains. Step three: file a compliance incident per GDPR/PCI/HIPAA and notify the data protection officer; the 72-hour GDPR breach notification clock starts when the leak is confirmed. Step four: add a preventive control — a log-scanning job that runs daily across the aggregator looking for PII patterns (regex for emails, Luhn-valid card numbers) and alerts on any match. Step five: add a code-review checklist item requiring PII review on every new log statement. Netflix's "data classification" library does this automatically at the logger level, hashing PII before it ever leaves the process.

**Visual:**
```
1. Patch logger to scrub PII at source (emails, cards, SSN)
2. Delete/rotate affected aggregator storage
3. File compliance incident (GDPR 72h clock starts)
4. Daily PII scan across aggregator (regex + Luhn)
5. Code-review checklist item on every new log statement
```

### Q7. You are asked to choose between Elasticsearch and Loki for a 200-engineer company ingesting 5 TB of logs per day. How do you decide?
**Answer:** The decision hinges on query patterns and budget. If engineers mostly know which service and time window they want to investigate — the common case in incident response — Loki's label-based indexing is sufficient and 10–100x cheaper than Elasticsearch for the same volume, because it stores compressed chunks in object storage and indexes only a handful of labels. At 5 TB/day, Loki's storage cost might be $0.023/GB/month on S3 (about $3,500/month for 30-day retention) versus Elasticsearch's 3–5x indexing overhead plus the cost of large RAM-heavy nodes (easily $30K–$50K/month). If, however, the team frequently needs full-text forensic search across unknown fields — "find every log line that mentions a specific error string anywhere in the fleet" — Elasticsearch's inverted index answers in seconds where Loki takes minutes. A pragmatic 2024 pattern is hybrid: Loki for the bulk of operational logs, Elasticsearch for a sampled subset (errors and WARNs only) where forensic search matters. For a 200-engineer company without dedicated observability staff, Loki + Grafana is usually the right call.

**Visual:**
```
5 TB/day ingestion:
  Elasticsearch: 3-5x index overhead, $30-50K/mo, fast full-text
  Loki:          label index only, ~$3.5K/mo S3, slower substring
  Hybrid:        Loki for bulk + ES for errors subset (best of both)
```
